scope: Nine original study questions: three distinctions and one changed situation for each of six signs. Not official exam questions, a pass prediction, or a driving-instructor assessment.

diagnosis.prompt: Two approaches look empty. One has STOP and the other YIELD. Which difference still matters?

options.text: STOP requires a complete stop; YIELD requires giving way and stopping when necessary.
options.why: The control determines the first action. Both approaches still require checking for a safe gap.

options.text: Both require a stop only when another road user is already visible.
options.why: This treats STOP as conditional. An apparently empty road does not remove the complete-stop requirement.

options.text: STOP controls vehicles; YIELD gives vehicles priority over pedestrians.
options.why: YIELD does not grant priority. Pedestrians and conflicting traffic still need to be checked.

applications.prompt: There is a stop line, no visible traffic, and a clear view. What must happen before you enter?

options.text: Stop completely before the line, then check and proceed only when safe.
options.why: The line establishes where to stop. A clear view helps the next decision; it does not cancel the stop.

options.text: Slow to walking speed at the line, then proceed if the road stays clear.
options.why: A very slow roll is still not a complete stop. Checking for traffic and obeying STOP are separate duties.

options.text: Stop only after crossing the line so you can confirm the road is clear.
options.why: The scenario already gives a clear view. Crossing the marked line first is not the required stopping position.

applications.prompt: At YIELD, a pedestrian is crossing your intended path. Which action follows the sign's meaning?

options.text: Give way, stopping if necessary, and proceed only after the conflict clears.
options.why: YIELD is not a promise that you can keep moving. Giving way can require a complete stop.

options.text: Keep rolling slowly because only a STOP sign can require a complete stop.
options.why: This confuses a conditional stop with no stop. The pedestrian conflict makes stopping necessary if you cannot otherwise give way.

options.text: Stop for a fixed count, then enter even if the pedestrian is still crossing.
options.why: A count does not create a safe gap or transfer priority. The conflict must clear before you proceed.

diagnosis.prompt: What is the useful difference between DO NOT ENTER at an entrance and WRONG WAY farther along a one-way road?

options.text: One prohibits entry from this direction; the other flags travel in the wrong direction.
options.why: DO NOT ENTER stands on its own. A later WRONG WAY sign is not permission to pass the entry control.

options.text: Both apply only after you have passed the entrance and seen oncoming traffic.
options.why: Waiting for oncoming traffic or a second warning defeats the entry restriction.

options.text: The first prohibits parking; the second requires a U-turn at the sign.
options.why: Neither meaning follows. They address direction of travel, and the sign alone cannot select a safe turning maneuver.

applications.prompt: Your navigation suggests a turn, but DO NOT ENTER faces you at that entrance. No WRONG WAY sign is visible. What follows?

options.text: Do not enter there; choose a legal route rather than waiting for another warning.
options.why: A navigation suggestion and an absent second sign do not override the entry control facing you.

options.text: Enter cautiously because the restriction needs a second sign to be valid.
options.why: DO NOT ENTER does not depend on seeing WRONG WAY farther along the road.

options.text: Enter if no approaching vehicle is visible, then check the next sign.
options.why: An empty view is not an exception to the entry restriction. The decision belongs before entry.

applications.prompt: After turning, you face WRONG WAY. What can you conclude from that sign, without inventing a maneuver for this road?

options.text: Your direction is wrong; do not continue against traffic and correct the situation safely and legally.
options.why: Recognize the direction error first. The available space, traffic, controls and local rules determine how it can be corrected.

options.text: Only the lane nearest the sign is wrong, so moving sideways always fixes it.
options.why: The sign does not establish that a neighboring lane is safe or lawful for your direction.

options.text: The sign authorizes an immediate U-turn regardless of traffic or restrictions.
options.why: A direction warning is not a blanket exception to safe and legal maneuvering requirements.

diagnosis.prompt: Both signs are yellow. Which distinction should guide your preparation?

options.text: MERGE warns of joining traffic; LANE ENDS warns that an existing lane ends ahead.
options.why: Color identifies a warning family, while the diagram identifies the particular conflict.

options.text: Both guarantee that your own lane ends on the side shown in every illustration.
options.why: A merge warning does not itself remove your lane. Read the actual diagram rather than memorizing a universal side.

options.text: Both give your vehicle priority and require the adjacent driver to stop.
options.why: Neither warning grants that priority. A safe response still depends on traffic, markings and applicable rules.

applications.prompt: You are on the main road and see this warning before an entrance ramp. Which preparation fits the information given?

options.text: Watch for traffic joining from the ramp and manage speed and space for the conflict.
options.why: Joining traffic is the warning. It does not, by itself, say your existing lane disappears.

options.text: Leave your lane immediately because this symbol means it ends at the ramp.
options.why: That substitutes a lane-reduction meaning for a joining-traffic warning and ignores whether a lane change is safe.

options.text: Keep the same gap because the sign guarantees entering traffic will stop.
options.why: A warning cannot guarantee another driver's behavior. Observation and space management still matter.

applications.prompt: A LANE ENDS sign is ahead. What must you establish before deciding how to position your vehicle?

options.text: Which lane the actual diagram and markings show ending, and whether a safe merge is available.
options.why: The warning identifies a lane reduction. The actual road and symbol establish the affected lane; traffic conditions establish the available gap.

options.text: That the same side always ends as in the practice picture, regardless of the posted diagram.
options.why: A generic study illustration cannot override a different lane configuration on the road.

options.text: That a ramp must be joining, so the number of existing lanes cannot change.
options.why: That is the opposite confusion: a lane reduction can occur without an entering ramp.
